papers.title: Road Pricing under Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Congestion pricing policies are widely debated and critics often argue that toll costs outweigh congestion relief. We show theoretically that welfare gains depend on two forces: the extent of driver heterogeneity—both in preferences and in exposure to highly demanded roads and times of day—and the extent of revenue recycling. We quantify the impact of both forces using data from a large-scale experiment that tracked driving behavior with and without usage-based congestion pricing incentives for nearly 10,000 drivers over two years. Using a model of time-varying traffic equilibrium with heterogeneous drivers and a granular road network, we show that a congestion pricing policy using the experiment's price schedule would raise welfare by as much as adding a new lane to every highway and would raise enough revenue to fully compensate losers. Moreover, the extent of driver heterogeneity entails that optimal prices can improve net welfare with only a small fraction of toll revenue.

papers.title: Gains from Trade in Gun Policy: A Compensation-Based Benchmark
papers.abstract: Policies restricting gun sales face substantial political opposition and constitutional constraints. In this paper, we ask how costly it would be to induce potential hand-gun buyers to choose less lethal alternatives. Pairing stated-choice experiments with a behavioral model of firearm choice, we estimate the payments required to induce substitution away from handguns toward long guns or no gun purchase. We then compare these payments with the resulting mortality benefits. We find substantial gains from trade: many prospective handgun buyers require relatively little compensation to switch and targeted compensation can avert homicides at a social cost well below conventional estimates of the value of a statistical life. The extent to which these gains can be realized through compensation, however, depends on the state’s information about which consumers would change their choices and at what price. Without this information, uniform subsidies pay consumers who would choose an alternative anyway and overcompensate those willing to switch for less, sharply increasing government expenditure and reducing the optimal scale of compensation.

papers.title: Survival versus Scale: The Effects of Critical Access Hospital Designation
papers.abstract: The Critical Access Hospital (CAH) program, established under the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, provides cost-based Medicare reimbursement to small rural hospitals in exchange for limits on inpatient capacity and service scope. We estimate the effects of CAH designation on hospital finances, capacity, and organizational outcomes using a synthetic difference-in-differences design that exploits the staggered 1999– 2002 rollout of state-level CAH availability. We find that CAH designation raises operating margins by three to four percentage points, with no change in liquidity or capital investment, as cost-based reimbursement sustains revenue while expenses fall with scale. Designation also reduces inpatient scale, with significant declines in total beds, obstetric capacity, and nursing staff. Emergency department visits also decline meaningfully, while outpatient volume is largely unchanged. At the same time, CAH designation reduces hospital closures, with no meaningful effect on mergers. These results point to a “survival versus scale” tradeoff across hospitals within a state, wherein designation-based subsidies avert closure for a small number of hospitals while inducing widespread inpatient downsizing among the many more hospitals that convert. Because converting hospitals shed more inpatient capacity than averted closures preserve, the program may reduce aggregate rural inpatient capacity even as it keeps hospitals open.
